item.title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)
item.medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper
item.museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
item.lesson: The most reproduced image in art history is not a painting but a print — one design from Hokusai's series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, produced in the thousands and sold for about the price of a bowl of noodles. Hokusai was around seventy when he made it, signing himself 'the old man crazy about painting.' The claw-tipped wave rears over three fishing boats whose crews bend flat to their oars; in the trough, tiny and immovable, sits Fuji — the sacred mountain the series is nominally about, here dwarfed by a moment of water. The blue is Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment newly imported from Europe, and the composition's flat planes and daring cropping flowed back the other way: when Japan reopened to trade in the 1850s, these prints hit Paris like weather, reshaping Monet, Degas, and van Gogh (who wrote about the wave in his letters). Debussy kept one on his wall while composing La Mer. One image, moving both directions around the planet.
item.lookFor: Look at the foam: Hokusai draws it as claws reaching for the boats — and then find how the wave's curve exactly cradles distant Fuji, so the mountain sits inside the sea's open mouth.
